video_title: Hedgeye Investing Summit Fall 2026 | Danielle DiMartino Booth, Founder/CEO, QI Research
gist: Danielle DiMartino Booth tells Hedgeye's Keith McCullen that Fed Chair Worsh is giving heavy forward guidance while hiking into a margin squeeze, with record small-business and corporate bankruptcies, junk-like AI financing and a likely panicked pivot to cuts. They also discuss Bessent, the dollar, and youth employment.

insights.claim: Fed Chair Worsh says he opposes forward guidance yet delivered heavy forward guidance at Jackson Hole and after the September 16 FOMC, hitching himself to core PCE inflation before his inflation task force reported any findings.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: Worsh's communication is inconsistent with his stated framework, making Fed reaction function harder to anchor.

insights.claim: After the September 16 FOMC, the bond market priced a 39% probability of an October 28 hike because every dot pointed to one more 2026 hike; Worsh's remarks then pushed markets to price the October hike in.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: Chair commentary, not the dots, moved October hike odds.

insights.claim: Other officials pushed back on Worsh: Waller said he expects several more hikes (plural) and that dropping forward guidance is like throwing the baby out with the bathwater; Williams and Vice Chair Jefferson spoke, and hike odds went from 80% to 20% after both vice chairs spoke.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: Forward guidance is alive via the vice chairs and Waller, not Worsh alone; watch them for odds swings.

insights.claim: Worsh obtained a unanimous FOMC vote, with Bowman not dissenting, which Booth reads as him listening to staff, though she thinks he is not a strong chair and his relationships with other officials are not coordinated.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: Uncoordinated Fed voices raise rate-path volatility.

themes.theme: Rate hikes, credit and Fed put

insights.claim: Small business bankruptcies are up 63% year-over-year, and larger corporate bankruptcies are running at a 15-year high by count; severity of individual bankruptcies is not yet there ('the next part of the movie').
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: Credit stress is building under an AI-dominated equity narrative; size of failures is the next leg.

insights.claim: A law change just raised the bankruptcy liability threshold to roughly 7.5 million dollars, easing small business and personal bankruptcy filings going forward.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: Expect further filings growth.

insights.claim: Per S&P, May, June and July each had more than 70 bankruptcies of companies with liabilities of 2 million or more, a pace not seen since 2010 outside 2020.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: The bankruptcy cycle is advanced yet ignored by the market.

insights.claim: Most defaults in recent years have come through distressed debt exchanges rather than bankruptcies, which generate bank fees, and a large majority eventually end in restructuring anyway.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: Reported default rates understate true stress.

insights.claim: High yield default probability is running very close to investment grade default probability; SoftBank, which most would assume investment grade, issued 11 billion dollars of junk debt at a 9.75% coupon.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: Credit quality boundaries are blurring; AI financing is paying junk-like coupons.

insights.claim: Keith McCullen is short long-term Treasuries, HYG and LQD, plus long bond volatility (MOVE); he notes rates and credit are now both being shorted and that MOVE at 105-110 is a lower high versus history, but above certain thresholds MOVE reflects credit rather than Treasury volatility.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullen
insights.so_what: Positioning is crowded short duration and credit; MOVE thresholds signal when credit breaks.

insights.claim: Triple-C spreads gapping out to about 1,000 basis points last week are Booth's proxy for private credit stress, since private credit is less creditworthy than junk bonds; further hikes would extend stress from commercial real estate into the 15.7 trillion corporate bond market.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: Triple-C spreads are the stress gauge to watch.
insights.quote: Triple C's gapping out to a thousand basis points last week told us we have problems

insights.claim: Historically, Treasuries and gold started bull markets after the final stage of hiking and stock crashes (2000 10-year at 6.8% then collapsed; 2007 at 5.3% then 1.4% by 2012), but McCullen says more steps remain: at least two more accelerating CPI prints and the next hikes must be priced in.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullen
insights.so_what: The catalyst for lower yields is completing the hiking cycle, so patience before covering shorts.

insights.claim: Booth expects the Fed's eventual shift to cuts to be panicked rather than measured, and that policymakers cannot allow the credit system to blow up, comparing it to Powell in late 2018.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: Bears should respect the risk that hikes flip abruptly to aggressive cuts and possibly QE.
insights.quote: And for the Fed to start cutting rates, it's not going to be measured. It's going to be panicked.

insights.claim: The Street's base case is that the Fed will buy stocks, and Booth warns a Wall Street campaign for the Fed to buy equities would end capitalism and anger young buyers hoping to buy homes and stocks cheaply.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: A policy backstop for equities is consensus, so its absence is a risk.
insights.quote: That is the street's base case. The Fed will buy stocks.

insights.claim: Rest of the world has been selling US Treasuries while piling into US corporates and the AI trade, so a credit accident would not stay isolated in the US.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: Global transmission raises the odds of coordinated central bank action.

themes.theme: Housing, wealth skew and policy errors

insights.claim: Money market fund assets of about 8 trillion are as concentrated in the top 1% as the stock market, so the rate hike was a home run for the wealthy earning risk-free yields near 6% while others are not.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: Hikes widen the K-shaped divide and may not slow the top cohort's spending.
insights.quote: for the top 1% this rate hike was a home run

insights.claim: Booth calls the Fed's second round of mortgage-backed securities buying worse than the first because it further distorted housing, but a 7.5% 30-year fixed mortgage could finally force seller capitulation and clear housing prices.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: Harsh policy may produce overdue clearing in housing, multifamily and CRE.

insights.claim: The era of extend and pretend in commercial real estate is ending: the biggest banks have sold problem CRE loans to private credit while small and regional banks cannot, and Booth calls clearing prices in office, multifamily and residential a good thing.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: Regional bank CRE exposure is a pressure point.

insights.claim: Margins are being squeezed: Pepsi said it cannot pass through higher costs, the PPI for trade services shows a big margin squeeze, and regional Fed surveys show prices paid rising; American and United cut capacity because they cannot fill the back of the plane.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: Cost pass-through is impaired by gas and utility bills, so hikes into slowing demand are an error.

insights.claim: Booth says 80% of stocks are down 20% or more, 89% of the Russell 3000 is down since June, and the S&P 500 ex-AI is down 5% since August; headline earnings peaked in Q2, and next year S&P earnings face a base effect and will be a train wreck.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: Short single stocks with cost pressure and weak balance sheets; high dividends may be fool's yield.

insights.claim: McCullen projects September and October CPI in the high 3s and inflation cut in half next year, and keeps shorts in industrials and bad balance sheets until the Fed starts a cut cycle.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullen
insights.so_what: Timing: stay short through the hikes, cover as cuts approach.

insights.claim: Indirect and direct bidders took 97.5% of yesterday's 10-year Treasury auction, a number never seen before.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: Auction demand is dominated by institutional buyers.
insights.quote: indirect and direct biders took down 97.5% of yesterday's 10-year Treasury action

insights.claim: Booth thinks Bessent and Worsh are not coordinating now, but would be on the phone arranging swap lines if something goes wrong; Bessent wants the Treasury to have more power in emergencies, believes in Fed independence and is opposed to QE.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: Coordination arrives only when crisis hits.

insights.claim: Bessent could tweak rules on how passive fixed income funds buy Treasuries to accelerate declines in long-end yields, though he would have to choose to do so.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: A Treasury lever exists to cap long yields.

insights.claim: Booth says a blue wave in the midterms could prompt Bessent to leave, but if a credit crisis hits, emerging markets and sovereigns issue emergency debt in dollars and she wants Bessent in the seat as a markets-savvy figure; she dismisses de-dollarization and notes the dollar has been a great long, with no history saying it does not break out in a quad four slowdown.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: Long dollar remains the crisis hedge; ignore de-dollarization narratives for trading.

themes.theme: Labor, AI and the next generation

insights.claim: Booth doubts Worsh's AI productivity miracle: employees are more productive under threat, but companies have executed AI without understanding how, and individual uptake, especially outside the US, has little money in it; she sees an AI leverage miracle instead.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: Fed's disinflation-through-AI premise is questionable; AI financing leverage is the risk.

insights.claim: Booth objects to the Fed's break-even unemployment rate implying the US can create zero jobs a month, arguing young people want to work, and McCullen says his interns are the most qualified cohort he has seen but will struggle to find Wall Street jobs.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: Weak entry-level hiring is a social and political risk into 2028.

insights.claim: Booth fears a 2028 pendulum swing pitting Silicon Valley's agenda (including universal basic income) against hard-working Texans and Connecticut residents who reject socialism, and says AI leaders asked this administration for help only because they want no guardrails.
insights.speaker: Danielle DiMartino Booth
insights.so_what: Political backlash against AI wealth concentration is a longer-dated risk.
